mcqs.question: What input causes the expand-around-center approach to hit its O(n²) worst case?
options: A string of all identical characters, like "aaaa...a", where every center's expansion runs nearly the full string length
A string with no repeated characters at all
A string that contains no palindromes longer than length 1
A string shorter than 10 characters
mcqs.explanation: With all identical characters, every one of the n centers expands almost all the way to the string's edges, making the total work proportional to n times the average expansion length — genuinely O(n^2). A string with no repeats or no long palindromes gives short expansions everywhere, and short strings simply scale the same worst case down, not eliminate it.

mcqs.question: Why does handling odd-length and even-length palindromes as separate code paths tend to introduce bugs?
options: Even-length palindromes are mathematically impossible to detect correctly
It requires two entirely different algorithms with no shared logic
It roughly doubles the bookkeeping, and an off-by-one in the even-length branch can go unnoticed if test cases lean toward odd-length examples
Odd-length palindromes cannot be expanded around a single character
mcqs.explanation: Maintaining two expansion loops — one from a character, one from a gap between characters — doubles the surface area for subtle indexing mistakes, and a bug isolated to the even-length path is easy to miss if your test suite happens to favor odd-length palindromes. Both cases are entirely detectable and do share the same expand-and-compare logic; the separator trick just removes the need to keep them apart.

mcqs.question: After inserting separators between every character (and at both ends), what is true of every palindrome in the transformed string?
options: Every palindrome in the transformed string is odd-length, centered on either an original character or a separator
Every palindrome in the transformed string becomes even-length
Palindromes shorter than 3 characters disappear entirely
Only palindromes centered on separators remain valid
mcqs.explanation: The separator insertion is specifically designed so every palindrome — regardless of its original odd or even length — becomes odd-length in the transformed string, letting one uniform algorithm handle both cases via a single center-and-radius computation. Nothing disappears and separator-centered palindromes aren't privileged over character-centered ones — both are handled identically.

mcqs.question: In Manacher's algorithm, what does center and right track as the scan proceeds?
options: The alphabetically smallest palindrome found and its length
The rightmost-reaching palindrome discovered so far and its center, used to safely initialize the radius at future positions
The total number of palindromes found up to the current position
The two characters currently being compared in the innermost loop
mcqs.explanation: center and right record the palindrome that currently extends furthest to the right, which lets a later position i reuse its mirror's already-computed radius as a safe starting point rather than expanding from zero — exactly the reuse trick that gives the O(n) bound. It has nothing to do with alphabetical ordering, a running palindrome count, or the comparison indices themselves.

mcqs.question: Why must radius[i] be capped at (right - i) before using radius[mirror] as a starting value, rather than copying radius[mirror] directly?
options: Copying directly would run out of array bounds
The mirror's palindrome might extend past the current known boundary right, past which the mirror symmetry is no longer guaranteed to hold
The cap is only a performance optimization with no effect on correctness
radius[mirror] is always larger than the correct value, so capping just corrects an overestimate
mcqs.explanation: The mirror symmetry that justifies reusing radius[mirror] is only proven to hold inside the known palindrome span [l, r] — if the mirror's radius would reach past right, that portion is unverified, and blindly copying it can produce an incorrect radius. This is a correctness issue, not just a speed one, and it isn't about array bounds or radius[mirror] being systematically too large.

mcqs.question: You've found the maximum value in the radius array at index i with radius r, using the separator-padded transformed string. How do you recover the palindrome's length and starting index in the ORIGINAL string?
options: The original length is r, and the original starting index is (i - r) // 2
The original length is 2r, and the starting index is i - r
The original length and starting index are identical to the padded string's — no conversion is needed
The original length is r // 2, and the starting index is i
mcqs.explanation: Because the separator characters cancel out algebraically, the radius r in the padded string equals the palindrome's length in the original string directly, and dividing (i - r) by 2 converts the padded-string index back to the original string's coordinate space. Treating padded and original indices as identical, or using 2r/i-r, ignores exactly the separator-padding conversion this step exists to handle.
